extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (authors), especially graduate students and postdocs writing research papers
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for writing mathematical research papers clearly, with a focused subsection (4.2) giving a ranked list of citation wordings and what each implies about provenance and proof reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of mathematical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing a mathematical paper is both an act of recording mathematical content and a means of communication of one’s work. The clarity suffers the most, which affects everyone in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clarity as the primary goal of math writing; clarity is 'everything'. Be willing to use simplified or non‑pedantic wording if it improves understanding for native and especially non‑native English speakers. Minor grammar rule violations are acceptable when they improve clarity; copy editors can fix stylistic issues later.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to cite a single paper — overall scale
rubrics_metrics.description: The citation rules are almost as complicated as Chinese honorifics. The post presents a (incomplete) list of possible ways in the decreasing level of citation importance and/or proof reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose citation wording deliberately to reflect confidence in the cited source and the provenance of the result; the list (1)–(12) gives a spectrum from definitive attribution to mere claim or hearsay.

rubrics_metrics.name: “Roth proved Murakami’s conjecture in [Roth].”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phrasing signals a definitive, clear statement that the cited source contains the proof; best for indicating that the cited paper is the actual place where the proof appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: “Roth proved Murakami’s conjecture [Roth].”
rubrics_metrics.description: Roth proved the conjecture, possibly in a different paper, but this is likely a definitive version of the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implies the cited reference is the likely definitive source, though it might not literally be the exact place in which the proof first appeared.

rubrics_metrics.name: “Roth proved Murakami’s conjecture, see [Roth].”
rubrics_metrics.description: Roth proved the conjecture, but [Roth] can be anything from the original paper to the followup, to some kind of survey Roth wrote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a weaker attribution: the reference might be a survey or secondary source. Occasionally used when the original is unpublished and someone else first published the proof (possibly with attribution).

rubrics_metrics.name: “Roth proved Murakami’s conjecture [Roth], see also [Woolf].”
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparently Woolf also made an important contribution, perhaps extending it to greater generality, or fixing some major gaps or errors in [Roth].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to indicate the cited work and another source that refines, extends, or repairs the original argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: “Roth proved Murakami’s conjecture in [Roth] (see also [Woolf]).”
rubrics_metrics.description: Looks like [Woolf] has a complete proof of Roth, possibly fixing some minor errors in [Roth].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parenthetical 'see also' suggests [Woolf] is a definitive or corrective exposition relative to the original.

rubrics_metrics.name: “Roth proved Murakami’s conjecture (see [Woolf]).”
rubrics_metrics.description: Here [Woolf] is a definitive version of the proof, e.g. the standard monograph on the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when the cited parenthetical source is the reliable or standard exposition and the original may be less accessible or less polished.

rubrics_metrics.name: “Roth proved Murakami’s conjecture, see e.g. [Faulkner, Fitzgerald, Frost].”
rubrics_metrics.description: The result is important enough to be cited and its validity confirmed in several books/surveys. If there ever was a controversy whether Roth’s argument is an actual proof, it was resolved in Roth’s favor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists multiple expositions to indicate broad acceptance and availability of the result; may also signal laziness if the author couldn't find the precise primary source.

rubrics_metrics.name: “Roth proved Murakami’s conjecture (see e.g. [Faulkner, Fitzgerald, Frost]).”
rubrics_metrics.description: The result is probably classical or at least very well known. Here are books/surveys which all probably have statements and/or proofs. Neither the author nor the reader will ever bother to check.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when the result is so standard that detailed provenance is unnecessary; signals commonly known status.

rubrics_metrics.name: “Roth proved Murakami’s conjecture. Footnote: See [Mailer].”
rubrics_metrics.description: Most likely, the author never actually read [Mailer], nor has access to that paper. Or, perhaps, [Mailer] states that Roth proved the conjecture, but includes neither a proof nor a reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phrasing signals weak verification — the footnote points to a source that itself may not provide a proof; the author cannot independently verify the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: “Roth proved Murakami’s conjecture. Footnote: Love letter from H. Fielding to J. Austen, dated December 16, 1975.”
rubrics_metrics.description: This means that the letter likely exists and contains the whole proof or at least an outline of the proof. The author may or may not have seen it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates an obscure, possibly archival source that might contain the proof; the citation hints at provenance but accessibility is doubtful.

rubrics_metrics.name: “Roth proved Murakami’s conjecture. Footnote: Personal communication.”
rubrics_metrics.description: This means Roth has sent the author an email (or said over beer), claiming to have a proof. Or perhaps Roth’s student accidentally mentioned this while answering a question after the talk. The proof may or may not be correct and the paper may or may not be forthcoming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use with caution: personal communications are unverifiable by readers and signal tentative or unpublished provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: “Roth claims to have proved Murakami’s conjecture in [Roth].”
rubrics_metrics.description: Paper [Roth] has a well known gap which was never fixed even though Roth insists on it to be fixable; the author would rather avoid going on record about this; or [Roth] is a brief note with an unresolved gap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This wording signals skepticism about the correctness or completeness of the cited work; often followed by parenthetical references that explain the controversy or point to corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signal citation confidence explicitly in wording
rubrics_metrics.description: Across the examples: small changes in phrasing (in / , / see / see also / footnote / personal communication / claims) systematically convey different levels of confidence, provenance, and accessibility of a cited result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be deliberate in choosing citation phrasing to communicate whether the cited source is the original proof, a survey, a corrective exposition, an obscure source, or an unverifiable claim. Use parentheticals or citations like 'see also' to point readers to definitive expositions when the original is incomplete or inaccessible.
